raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy for symptomatic heart failure (HF) intended for patients who remain limited despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and who are not candidates for, or have not responded to, conventional electrical resynchronization. Contemporary HF guidelines emphasize rapid optimization of foundational pharmacotherapy and selective use of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) devices [1], [2]. CRT has strong evidence in patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and electrical dyssynchrony, improving symptoms, remodeling, hospitalization, and survival in appropriately selected patients [3], [4], [5]. However, many patients with persistent New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III symptoms have narrow QRS complexes, modestly reduced LVEF, or inadequate CRT response; CCM was developed to address this therapeutic gap.

CCM differs mechanistically from pacing and CRT. The device delivers relatively high-voltage, biphasic, non-excitatory impulses to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, timed so that no new action potential or ventricular depolarization is initiated. Acute human data showed that CCM can enhance LV contractile state without a measurable increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [6]. Early combined-device experience also suggested technical feasibility in patients failing CRT [7]. The pivotal double-blind European FIX-HF-4 study showed that active CCM periods were associated with better peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores than sham periods, supporting a biologic effect beyond placebo, although the crossover design and procedural implantation limited interpretation [8].

The clinical development program then moved toward larger and more pragmatic studies. The FIX-HF-5 design described a broad population with advanced systolic HF and narrow QRS [9]. A prespecified analysis of FIX-HF-5 identified stronger effects in patients with LVEF between 25% and 45%, a range subsequently used for confirmatory testing [10]. The FIX-HF-5C design refined endpoints, emphasizing peak VO₂ rather than ventilatory anaerobic threshold and incorporating Bayesian borrowing from prior data [11]. In FIX-HF-5C, 160 patients with NYHA III/ambulatory IV symptoms, QRS <130 ms, and LVEF 25–45% were randomized to CCM plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone; CCM improved peak VO₂, MLHFQ, NYHA class, and 6-minute walk distance, with an acceptable device-related safety profile [12]. FIX-HF-5C2 evaluated a 2-lead Optimizer Smart system, eliminating the atrial lead and demonstrating similar signal delivery, improved peak VO₂ versus historical controls, and fewer device-related adverse events than the 3-lead system [13].

Meta-analyses generally show consistent symptomatic and functional benefit but do not establish mortality reduction. A trial-level meta-analysis found MLHFQ improvement without statistically significant differences in HF hospitalization, arrhythmia, or mortality over short follow-up [14]. An individual patient data meta-analysis found modest but significant gains in peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and MLHFQ, effects clinically comparable to other symptom-directed HF interventions [15]. Mechanistic reviews and translational studies support effects on calcium cycling, phosphorylation of contractile proteins, sympathetic tone, and reverse molecular remodeling [16]. Exploratory analyses suggest that patients with LVEF 40–45% may also benefit, particularly in exercise capacity [17].

Real-world data broaden the evidence base but remain observational. A large Optimizer Smart registry reported sustained improvements in quality of life, LVEF, hospitalizations, and survival compared with risk-model predictions [18]. Epidemiologic screening studies suggest that only a minority of unselected HF patients meet current CCM criteria, but that the eligible group represents an important population with persistent symptoms and limited device options [19]. Interest is expanding beyond HFrEF: a pilot HFpEF study reported improved health status at 24 weeks [20], and the AIM HIGHer program is testing CCM in higher-EF HF populations [21]. Practical implementation requires expertise in lead positioning, sensing windows, programming, charging, and troubleshooting [22]. Reviews emphasize that CCM should complement—not replace—GDMT, defibrillator therapy when indicated, and CRT when criteria are met [23], [24]. Recent single-arm and observational syntheses reinforce improvement in functional status but also highlight the need for adequately powered, sham-controlled trials with hospitalization and mortality endpoints [25], [26]. Preclinical HFpEF and metabolic-remodeling data provide a rationale for broader testing [27], while critical editorials caution that symptom improvement must be weighed against procedural risk, cost, and uncertain hard outcomes [28]. Long-term single-center and small clinical series are encouraging but hypothesis-generating [29], [30]. Overall, CCM is best viewed as a targeted, symptom-improving device therapy for carefully selected patients with persistent HF symptoms, narrow QRS, and LVEF roughly 25–45%, with future trials needed to define durability, cost-effectiveness, and outcome benefit.
